_readme: THE LIVE TO-DO LIST, AS DATA. This file is the source; to-do.md's table and the
Handbook's ranking control both read it. Edit here, not in two places.
Every item must carry all five fields the list's own rules demand — score, why,
risk, askedBy, touches — and tests/unit/toDoItems.test.js fails the build if one
is missing. That guard is the whole reason this file exists: an item missing a
field is a note, and notes are what produced two pieces of unrequested work on
ORDER IS MIKE'S RANKING. The array order is the order on screen. It is not
computed from the score, and it must never be re-sorted by a script or a session.
Where his order and the score disagree, his order wins and the score stays
visible so the disagreement is on the page.
SCORE — 5 security/privacy/data integrity · 4 the user is worse off · 3 helps
sell the package · 2 robustness · 1 internal only · 0 is not filed, it is

items.name: Put the ranking control into the Handbook
items.why: The ranking table Mike used on 2026-08-15 was a standalone drawing with its items typed in by hand, and its Save only put text in a box to copy out. The Handbook already has the round trip it needs — edit, survives a reload, Save writes a real file to Downloads — so the control belongs there.
items.risk: The ranking and the notes Mike applies cannot reach the repository except by hand, so his own ordering decays back into prose the moment a session ends.

askedBy.detail: 2026-08-15, session 57 — "the last session developed a ranking system that I could apply and I could add notes. It was never coded into the handbook as we ran out of context." He also asked for it to be split across 2-3 sessions so it cannot be lost again.

items.touches: This file, scripts/build-handbook.js, scripts/handbook-shell.html, to-do.md's table.
items.note: SCORE 1 AND RANKED FIRST — the disagreement is deliberate and stays visible. No customer will ever see the Handbook, so by the table it is internal. Mike asked for it and ranked it now; his call beats the score, and the score stays on the page rather than being quietly inflated to justify the position.

phases.what: The nine items become data, with a guard test on the five fields.
The Handbook's To-Do page renders the ranking control instead of prose.
The Save file comes back into this data, and to-do.md's table is generated from it.

items.name: Send the master team the release number
items.why: v0.8.0 is tagged and pushed and nobody outside has been told it exists. They cannot pull what they do not know about; v0.6.0 was never pulled at all.
items.risk: The release round does not start. Every piece of feedback we need is deferred by however long this sits.
items.touches: Everything already built. Three lines: pull the tag v0.8.0, no npm install this time, read design/UAT-LOAD-PACK.md first.
items.note: The integration email that goes with it is already drafted at design/MASTER-TEAM-INTEGRATION-EMAIL.md — five questions. Do not re-derive it.

items.name: One handover story for the master team
items.why: The merged app's own handover documents still describe a separate standalone application.
items.risk: The master team reads documents describing an app that no longer exists and builds the tiers above it wrongly.

askedBy.detail: Nobody outside asked. Kept because the master team genuinely receives the wrong documents — say so if you would rather it went.

items.touches: The Collaborate handover documents, the UAT load pack.

items.name: advisor_note — one line from you
items.why: The profitability_feasibility / pf_awareness node in Mike's own logic tree carries a real instruction that reaches the AI nowhere — "This determines the delivery method. Do not use Trial Fit on an unaware client — it will cause map shock. Do not use Cautious Reveal on a motivated client — it will feel slow and condescending." formatNodeForPrompt does not read it.
items.risk: The AI keeps choosing a delivery method against Mike's own written instruction.

askedBy.detail: Found by us, in Mike's own logic-tree content. Not fixed unasked because emitting a new field changes what the model is told.

items.touches: formatNodeForPrompt, every recommendation using that branch.
items.note: The open question for Mike: should it be emitted the same gated way `recommendation` now is?

items.name: Seminar's seven lines — reword toward Public Speaking
items.why: The gate correctly refuses to name a tool nobody can open, so seven lines of coaching never reach an adviser.
items.risk: A table of coaching advisers simply are not receiving. This is not tidying.

askedBy.detail: His to reword, carried since session 48

items.touches: Mentor Hub → Logic Tables → Get Seminar.

items.name: The education-gate wording
items.why: The behaviour is already ruled — on low client literacy the adviser is asked whether to apply education-first or see what is technically needed, reasoning shown either way. Only the on-screen words are missing.
items.risk: It stays uncoded. Advisers keep getting advice pitched over a client's head.
items.touches: The Advisory Staircase, the pre-recommendation prompt.

items.name: Make the coaching reference inherit
items.why: Its fifteen rows already carry stable ids; it simply never joined the inheritance mechanism, and its firm side is append-only.
items.risk: A firm cannot tailor its own coaching reference the way it can everything else — the cascade has a hole in it.

askedBy.detail: From Mike's tier-cascade design, but nobody asked for this row specifically.

items.touches: resolveInheritedRows, the firm overlay, the coaching reference screen.

items.name: Prove a Handbook edit survives a reload
items.why: Edit-persistence is proven in code and has never been seen working in a browser.
items.risk: The one-link Handbook Mike asked for may not actually keep an edit, and we would not know.
items.note: One click, and it has to be his: this machine has no browser automation, so no session can prove it for him.

items.name: Flip engine-strict back on
items.why: Still false. Two transitive packages (consola, node-releases) over-declare their Node requirement and need pinning down first.
items.risk: The Node 14.15 lock is not actually enforced at install time, so a future install can drift off the Stack Constitution silently.
items.note: Reinstall is overnight-only on this machine and there is a documented safe procedure — follow it rather than a plain npm install.

items.why: Somebody outside is waiting on an answer.
